topic: physical properties used to identify substances

easy.text: Which of these is a physical property of a substance?

options.feedback: Correct -- melting point can be observed without changing the substance into something new.
Flammability describes how a substance reacts (burns) to become a new substance, making it a chemical property.
This describes a chemical change, making it a chemical property, not physical.
Rusting forms a new substance, making this a chemical property, not physical.

medium.text: Two clear liquids look identical. Which physical property would best help identify which one is water?

options.feedback: Correct -- comparing each liquid's boiling point to water's known 100°C can help identify it without altering its identity.

options.text: Whether it reacts with a strong acid
options.feedback: Testing a reaction would cause a chemical change, going beyond simply observing a physical property.
Flammability is a chemical property, not a physical one, and involves an actual reaction.
This describes a chemical interaction, not a physical property of the liquid itself.

hard.text: Which TWO of the following are physical properties, rather than chemical properties?

options.feedback: Correct -- density can be measured without changing the substance's identity.
Correct -- color is observable without any chemical transformation.
This describes a chemical property, since it involves forming a new substance.

options.text: Toxicity when combined with another chemical
options.feedback: This describes how the substance reacts with something else, making it a chemical property.
Decomposition creates new substances, making this a chemical property.

easy.hard: This property can be observed or measured without turning the substance into something chemically different.
easy.medium: This is a property you can measure without causing a chemical reaction.
easy.easy: This is something you can observe about a substance without changing what it's made of.

medium.hard: Look for a measurable characteristic that distinguishes the liquid without triggering any chemical transformation.
medium.medium: Compare a measurable physical characteristic, like the temperature at which each liquid boils.
medium.easy: Compare the temperature at which each liquid starts to boil.

hard.hard: Two of these five can be observed or measured with no chemical transformation occurring; the other three all describe how the substance reacts or transforms into something new.
hard.medium: Two of these can be measured without any reaction happening; the rest all involve the substance changing into something new.
hard.easy: Two of these you can observe without anything reacting or changing into something new.

easy.text: In a synthesis reaction, what generally happens?

options.text: Two or more simple substances combine to form one more complex substance
options.feedback: Correct -- synthesis reactions build a single, more complex product from simpler starting materials.

options.text: One complex substance breaks apart into simpler substances
options.feedback: That describes a decomposition reaction, the opposite of synthesis.
A synthesis reaction always results in a new combined substance being formed.

options.text: A substance changes color without reacting
options.feedback: This doesn't describe an actual chemical combination happening.

medium.text: Which equation represents a decomposition reaction?

options.feedback: Correct -- one compound (water) breaks down into two simpler substances.
This combines simpler substances into one compound, making it a synthesis reaction instead.
This swaps components between two compounds, which is a different reaction type (double replacement), not decomposition.
This is a combustion reaction, where a substance reacts with oxygen, not a simple breakdown of one compound.

hard.text: Heating calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) produces calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). What type of reaction is this?

options.feedback: Correct -- one starting compound breaks down into two separate simpler products.
Synthesis would combine multiple substances into one, but here one substance is breaking into two.
Single replacement involves one element swapping places with another in a compound, which isn't happening here.
Combustion specifically involves reacting with oxygen gas in a burning process, not simply heating a solid compound apart.

easy.hard: The direction of change here is toward combination, not toward breaking apart.
easy.medium: Multiple simpler starting materials come together into one final substance.
easy.easy: This reaction joins simpler things together into one bigger thing.

medium.hard: Look at whether one compound is being broken apart into two or more distinct products, versus multiple substances joining into one.
medium.medium: Look for the equation where a single starting compound splits into separate simpler products.
medium.easy: Look for the equation where one thing on the left breaks into two things on the right.

hard.hard: One starting compound is being broken apart into two distinct, simpler products, which is the defining pattern of this reaction type.
hard.medium: One compound breaking into two separate products is the key sign of this specific reaction type.
hard.easy: One substance splitting into two separate substances is the key clue here.

easy.text: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?

options.text: Speeds up the reaction without being consumed
options.feedback: Correct -- catalysts lower the energy needed for a reaction and come out of it unchanged.
Catalysts speed reactions up, they don't slow them down.

options.text: Gets permanently used up in the reaction
options.feedback: A defining feature of catalysts is that they are NOT consumed by the reaction.

options.text: Changes the final products of the reaction
options.feedback: Catalysts affect the reaction's speed, not what products ultimately form.

medium.text: How does increasing temperature generally affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.feedback: Correct -- higher temperature gives particles more energy, leading to more frequent and effective collisions.
Higher temperature generally speeds reactions up, not slows them down.

options.text: It has no effect on reaction rate
options.feedback: Temperature is actually one of the main factors affecting how fast a reaction proceeds.
Increased temperature speeds up most reactions rather than stopping them.

hard.text: Why does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction to occur
options.feedback: Correct -- a lower energy barrier means more particle collisions succeed in reacting per unit time.

options.text: It increases the temperature of the surroundings
options.feedback: A catalyst works by changing the reaction pathway, not simply by heating things up.

options.text: It adds more reactant molecules to the mixture
options.feedback: A catalyst doesn't add material to the reaction -- it changes how easily existing reactants can react.

options.text: It removes some of the products as they form
options.feedback: Removing products is a different technique entirely, unrelated to how catalysts function.

easy.hard: This substance participates in helping the reaction along but is chemically unchanged by the end.
easy.medium: This helps a reaction go faster but comes out the other side unchanged.
easy.easy: This makes a reaction happen faster without being used up itself.

medium.hard: More thermal energy means particles move and collide more frequently and forcefully.
medium.medium: More heat means particles move faster and collide more often, which speeds things up.
medium.easy: More heat makes molecules move faster, which usually speeds up reactions.

hard.hard: A catalyst provides an alternate reaction pathway requiring less energy input to get reactants over the energy barrier.
hard.medium: A catalyst provides an easier path for the reaction, requiring less energy to get it started.
hard.easy: A catalyst makes it easier for the reaction to get started, needing less energy overall.

easy.text: Which group of elements is known for being extremely unreactive?

options.feedback: Correct -- noble gases like helium and neon rarely form chemical bonds.
Alkali metals are actually highly reactive, the opposite of unreactive.
Halogens are quite reactive, especially with metals, not known for being unreactive.
Transition metals vary in reactivity but aren't specifically known as the unreactive group.

medium.text: Why are noble gases generally unreactive?

options.text: They already have a full outer electron shell
options.feedback: Correct -- a complete outer shell means they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.

options.text: They have no electrons at all
options.feedback: Noble gases do have electrons -- their stability comes from having a complete outer shell, not from lacking electrons.
Density isn't what determines chemical reactivity in this case.

options.text: They only exist at very high temperatures
options.feedback: Noble gases exist as gases at room temperature and their unreactivity isn't about temperature conditions.

hard.text: Which of the following best explains why noble gases are positioned in the far right column of the periodic table?

options.text: They share the property of having a complete valence electron shell, which places them together as a group
options.feedback: Correct -- elements are grouped by similar valence electron configurations, and noble gases uniquely share a full outer shell.

options.text: They were the first elements ever discovered
options.feedback: Discovery order isn't how the periodic table columns are organized.

options.text: They are the heaviest elements known
options.feedback: Noble gases include some very light elements, like helium, so weight isn't the organizing factor here.
Noble gases occur naturally in the atmosphere and elsewhere -- this isn't why they're grouped together.

easy.hard: This group's atoms rarely need to gain, lose, or share electrons with other atoms.
easy.medium: This group of elements almost never forms bonds with other elements.
easy.easy: This group of gases barely reacts with anything at all.

medium.hard: Their outermost energy level is already completely filled with electrons, removing the usual drive to bond.
medium.medium: Their outer shell of electrons is already completely full, so they don't need to bond.
medium.easy: Their outer shell of electrons is already full, so they don't need to react with anything.

hard.hard: Periodic table columns group elements sharing similar valence electron configurations -- noble gases uniquely share a complete outer shell, distinguishing them as a column.
hard.medium: Elements in the same column share a similar outer-electron setup -- noble gases all happen to have a full outer shell.
hard.easy: Elements in the same column of the table share similar electron setups -- these elements all have a full outer shell.

easy.text: What is a vertical column in the periodic table called?

options.feedback: Correct -- vertical columns are called groups (or families).
A period refers to a horizontal row, not a vertical column.
While 'block' is used for certain regions of the table, it isn't the term for a single vertical column.
'Series' isn't the standard term for a vertical column in the periodic table.

medium.text: Elements in the same period (row) of the periodic table share which of the following?

options.text: The same number of electron shells
options.feedback: Correct -- elements in a period all have the same number of occupied electron shells.
Elements in the same period actually vary widely in chemical properties -- that similarity is more true within a group.

options.text: The exact same number of valence electrons
options.feedback: Valence electron count increases across a period -- it's elements in the same group that typically share this.
Atomic mass increases across a period, it isn't shared equally among elements in a row.

hard.text: Why do elements within the same group (column) of the periodic table tend to have similar chemical properties?

options.text: They have the same number of valence electrons
options.feedback: Correct -- matching valence electron counts lead to similar bonding behavior and reactivity.

options.text: They have the same atomic mass
options.feedback: Atomic mass varies considerably down a group -- it's valence electron count that stays consistent.

options.text: They were all discovered in the same year
options.feedback: Discovery timing has no bearing on chemical behavior.

options.text: They all have the exact same number of electron shells
options.feedback: The number of electron shells actually increases going down a group -- that's a period-related pattern, not what defines a group.

easy.hard: This term describes elements arranged up and down, sharing similar outer-electron patterns.
easy.medium: This is the term for a column of elements stacked vertically.
easy.easy: This is the up-and-down column of elements in the table.

medium.hard: This shared trait relates to how many energy levels of electrons surround the nucleus, which increases moving down the table but stays consistent moving across a single row.
medium.medium: Elements across the same row share the same count of electron energy levels.
medium.easy: Elements in the same row all have the same number of electron shells.

hard.hard: The number of electrons in the outermost shell is what drives an element's bonding behavior, and this number stays consistent down a single column.
hard.medium: Elements in the same column all have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which drives similar reactivity.
hard.easy: Elements in the same column all have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

options.text: How much of a solute can dissolve in a solvent
options.feedback: Correct -- solubility measures the maximum amount of solute that will dissolve under given conditions.
Boiling speed relates to heat and pressure, not solubility.
Color isn't what solubility measures.
Container weight has nothing to do with how much solute can dissolve.

medium.text: For most solid solutes, how does increasing temperature typically affect their solubility in water?

options.feedback: Correct -- warmer water can typically dissolve more of most solid solutes, like sugar.
This is the general pattern for gases dissolving in liquids, but most solids become MORE soluble as temperature rises.

options.text: It has no effect on solubility at all
options.feedback: Temperature is actually one of the main factors that changes how much solute can dissolve.

options.text: It always makes the solute stop dissolving completely
options.feedback: Higher temperature typically helps more solute dissolve, not less.

hard.text: Unlike most solids, how does increasing temperature typically affect the solubility of gases in a liquid?

options.feedback: Correct -- warmer liquids hold LESS dissolved gas, which is why warm soda goes flat faster.

options.text: It increases the gas's solubility, just like with solids
options.feedback: Gases behave oppositely to most solids -- their solubility actually drops as temperature rises.

options.text: It has no effect on gas solubility
options.feedback: Temperature does affect gas solubility -- it just works in the opposite direction compared to most solids.

options.text: It turns the dissolved gas into a solid
options.feedback: The gas simply escapes the liquid as temperature rises -- it doesn't turn into a solid.

easy.hard: This term describes an upper limit on how much of one substance can mix into another before no more will dissolve.
easy.medium: This describes the maximum amount of a substance that will dissolve into a liquid.
easy.easy: This describes how much of something can dissolve in a liquid.

medium.hard: For most solids, added thermal energy helps break apart the solute's structure, generally allowing more to dissolve.
medium.medium: Warmer water usually lets more solid material dissolve into it.
medium.easy: Warmer water usually dissolves more sugar or salt than cold water.

hard.hard: Gas molecules have more kinetic energy at higher temperatures, making them more likely to escape the liquid rather than stay dissolved -- the opposite trend from solids.
hard.medium: Warmer liquids let dissolved gas escape more easily, unlike the trend seen with dissolved solids.
hard.easy: This is why a warm soda goes flat faster than a cold one -- heat lets the gas escape.
